appraisal_events.evidence: "le roi... a eu la bonté de se souvenir en m'apercevant à l'orchestre que j'avais eu l'honneur de le voir plusieurs jours à la cour de Bavière... Un aide de camp est venu me dire d'aller saluer Sa Majesté"
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois's self-narrated account of being personally recognized and summoned by the king casts him as a man favored by royalty, though the boastful, self-important framing of his own report tempers full narrator endorsement.

appraisal_events.evidence: "C'est tout simplement un coup de maître... il a été choisi à merveille, vous avez vu comme il a porté. Pour ma part j'y applaudis des deux mains."
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois delivers an extended, effusive encomium of the king's toast and political daring, but the pompous, cliché-laden diplomatic rhetoric (echoing the immediately preceding narratorial doubt about Norpois's evaluative criteria) invites ironic distance rather than a straightforward narrator-endorsed elevation of the king.

status_effects.explanation: Norpois's local standing rises modestly through his reported personal proximity to and recognition by the king, though the self-reported, self-congratulatory nature of the account tempers the effect.
The king is locally praised for political skill and eloquence, but the inflated, clichéd rhetoric in which the praise is delivered qualifies how strongly the passage endorses it.

ambiguities: The passage is entirely Norpois's quoted, self-important diplomatic speech; the immediately preceding narrator context signals skepticism about Norpois's evaluative criteria, which colors both his praise of the king and his account of royal favor toward himself, but the passage itself contains no explicit narratorial undercutting, so endorsement versus irony cannot be resolved with high confidence.
